messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arthur presents as a man who has spent a lifetime building walls. At sixty-six, he has a successful career as a software engineer, a long-standing marriage, and a quiet, orderly life that he has meticulously constructed to keep the past at bay. For over fifty years, he has managed the echoes of his childhood, but now, the echoes have become too loud to ignore. The trauma dates back to when he was seven, living with his uncle for a year. The punishments for minor infractions were severe and unpredictable. The memory that surfaces most often, unbidden and sharp, is of being locked in the basement. He can still feel the specific, damp cold of the concrete floor seeping through his thin pyjamas, a chill that has nothing to do with the ambient temperature. He remembers the frantic, rabbit-like thumping of his own heart against his ribs, a sound that seemed to fill the darkness as he waited, certain he would be forgotten there forever.

This history has left indelible marks on his sensory world. A draft from an overzealous office air conditioner can be enough to trigger it; the specific temperature on his skin catapults him back to that basement floor, and for a moment, he is seven years old again, helpless and terrified. Similarly, the normal sensation of his heart racing—whether from climbing a flight of stairs too quickly or the stress of a looming project deadline—is no longer a simple physiological response. For Arthur, the pounding in his chest is a direct line to that childhood terror, a signal that something dreadful is about to happen. His body seems to hold the memory more viscerally than his mind, reacting to perceived danger before he has even had time to consciously register a threat.

Over the decades, Arthur has learned to navigate a world he perceives as fundamentally unsafe. He has come to believe that constant vigilance is the only rational way to live, because you truly never know what can happen next. When entering any room, his eyes perform an unconscious, sweeping inventory of potential dangers, clocking heavy objects, sharp corners, or anything that could conceivably be used as a weapon. This internal threat assessment is as automatic to him as breathing. It has fostered a deep and abiding mistrust of others. He is certain that people, even those with good intentions, are ultimately unreliable and capable of causing harm. This conviction has made him feel like a permanent outsider, observing the easy camaraderie of his colleagues or the casual affection between other couples from behind an invisible barrier.

To manage this constant sense of threat, Arthur has systematically narrowed his life. Physical contact is the most difficult. An unexpected hand on his shoulder from a colleague can cause him to flinch with an alarm that is startling to everyone involved. He has learned to position himself in meetings to avoid anyone getting behind him. At home, he avoids being touched by his wife, a pattern that has, over many years, eroded the physical intimacy between them. What she sees as rejection, he experiences as a necessary act of self-preservation. He has also gradually withdrawn from social life. The team lunches and after-work drinks he used to attend became too fraught with the potential for unpredictable interactions, so he started making excuses. Now, he socialises with almost no one he knew before the event became so acute in his mind. He even finds himself avoiding his own reflection, averting his gaze from his own body, as if it is a separate entity that holds all the pain and fear he cannot bear to confront.

It was his wife, after another pained and disconnected evening, who finally gave him an ultimatum. Her tears, and her words about feeling married to a ghost, broke through the fortress he had built. Arthur is now seeking help, not with any grand hope of transformation, but with the quiet, desperate wish that he might be able to feel safe in his own skin, in his own home, for the first time in his life. He is terrified of dredging up the past, but what frightens him more is the prospect of living out the rest of his years as a stranger to the person who loves him most.
